entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 5 So 5:1-16 . 1. Answer to her prayer ( Is 65:24 ; Re 3:20 ). am come-- already ( So 4:16 ); "come" ( Ge 28:16 ). sister ... spouse-- As Adam's was created of his flesh, out of his opened side, there being none on earth on a level with him, so the bride out of the pierced Saviour ( Ep 5:30-32 ). have gathered ... myrrh-- His course was already complete; the myrrh, &c. ( Mt 2:11 ; 26:7-12; Joh 19:39 ), emblems of the indwelling of the anointing Holy Ghost, were already gathered. spice-- literally, "balsam." have eaten-- answering to her "eat" ( So 4:16 ). honeycomb-- distinguished here from liquid "honey" dropping from trees. The last supper, here set forth, is one of espousal, a pledge of the future marriage ( So 8:14 ; Re 19:9 ). Feasts often took place in gardens. In the absence of sugar, then unknown, honey was more widely used than with us. His eating honey with milk indicates His true, yet spotless, human nature from infancy ( Is 7:15 ); and after His resurrection ( Lu 24:42 ). my wine-- ( Joh 18:11 )--a cup of wrath to Him, of mercy to us, whereby God's Word and promises become to us "milk" ( Psa 19:10 ; 1Pe 2:2 ). "My" answers to "His" ( So 4:16 ). The myrrh (emblem, by its bitterness, of repentance), honey, milk (incipient faith), wine (strong faith), in reference to believers, imply that He accepts all their graces, however various in degree. eat-- He desires to make us partakers in His joy ( Is 55:1 , 2; Joh 6:53-57 ; 1Jo 1:3 ). drink abundantly-- so as to be filled ( Ep 5:18 ; as Hag 1:6 ). friends-- ( Joh 15:15 ). Canticle IV.-- (So 5: 2-8:4 )--From the Agony of Gethsemane to the Conversion of Samaria.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8254"/><div sID="gen13037" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8254"/>2. Sudden change of scene from evening to midnight, from a betrothal feast to cold repulse. He has gone from the feast alone; night is come; He knocks at the door of His espoused; she hears, but in sloth does not shake off half-conscious drowsiness; namely, the disciples' torpor (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.40-Matt.26.43">Mt 26:40-43</reference>), "the spirit willing, the flesh weak" (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.7.18-Rom.7.25">Ro 7:18-25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.16">Ga 5:16</reference>, 17, 24). Not total sleep. The lamp was burning beside the slumbering wise virgin, but wanted trimming (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.5-Matt.25.7">Mt 25:5-7</reference>). It is His voice that rouses her (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.6">Jon 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.14">Ep 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.20">Re 3:20</reference>). Instead of bitter reproaches, He addresses her by the most endearing titles, "my sister, my love," &c. Compare His thought of Peter after the denial (<reference osisRef="Mark.16.7">Mr 16:7</reference>).<div eID="gen13037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dew--</hi>which falls heavily in summer nights in the East (see <reference osisRef="Luke.9.58">Lu 9:58</reference>).<div eID="gen13038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13039" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drops of the night--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.22.2">Psa 22:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.22.44">Lu 22:44</reference>). His death is not expressed, as unsuitable to the allegory, a song of love and joy; <reference osisRef="Song.5.4">So 5:4</reference> refers to the scene in the judgment hall of Caiaphas, when Jesus Christ employed the cock-crowing and look of love to awaken Peter's sleeping conscience, so that his "bowels were moved" (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.61">Lu 22:61</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.62">62</reference>); <reference osisRef="Song.5.5">So 5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.5.6">6</reference>, the disciples with "myrrh," &c. (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.1">Lu 24:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.5">5</reference>), seeking Jesus Christ in the tomb, but finding Him not, for He has "withdrawn Himself" (<reference osisRef="John.7.34">Joh 7:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.13.33">13:33</reference>); <reference osisRef="Song.5.7">So 5:7</reference>, the trials by watchmen extend through the whole night of His withdrawal from Gethsemane to the resurrection; they took off the "veil" of Peter's disguise; also, literally the linen cloth from the young man (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.51">Mr 14:51</reference>); <reference osisRef="Song.5.8">So 5:8</reference>, the sympathy of friends (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.27">Lu 23:27</reference>).<div eID="gen13039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">undefiled--</hi>not polluted by spiritual adultery (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.4">Re 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.4">Jas 4:4</reference>). <div eID="gen13040" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8256"/><div sID="gen13044" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8256"/>4. A key in the East is usually a piece of wood with pegs in it corresponding to small holes in a wooden bolt within, and is put through a hole in the door, and thus draws the bolt. So Jesus Christ "puts forth His hand (namely, His Spirit, <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.14">Eze 3:14</reference>), by (Hebrew, 'from,' so in <reference osisRef="Song.2.9">So 2:9</reference>) the hole"; in "chastening" (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.2">Psa 38:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.14-Rev.3.22">Re 3:14-22</reference>, singularly similar to this passage), and other unexpected ways letting Himself in (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.61">Lu 22:61</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.62">62</reference>).<div eID="gen13044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bowels ... moved for him--</hi>It is His which are first troubled for us, and which cause ours to be troubled for Him (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.20">Jr 31:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.8">Ho 11:8</reference>). <div eID="gen13045" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8257"/><div sID="gen13046" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8257"/><hi type="bold">5. dropped with myrrh--</hi>The best proof a bride could give her lover of welcome was to anoint herself (the back of the hands especially, as being the coolest part of the body) profusely with the best perfumes (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.23">Ex 30:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.2.12">Es 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.7.17">Pr 7:17</reference>); "sweet-smelling" is in the Hebrew rather, "spontaneously exuding" from the tree, and therefore the best. She designed also to anoint Him, whose "head was filled with the drops of night" (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.1">Lu 24:1</reference>). The myrrh typifies bitter repentance, the fruit of the Spirit's unction (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.21">2Co 1:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen13046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13047" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">handles of the lock--</hi>sins which closed the heart against Him. <div eID="gen13047" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 5. dropped with myrrh-- The best proof a bride could give her lover of welcome was to anoint herself (the back of the hands especially, as being the coolest part of the body) profusely with the best perfumes ( Ex 30:23 ; Es 2:12 ; Pr 7:17 ); "sweet-smelling" is in the Hebrew rather, "spontaneously exuding" from the tree, and therefore the best. She designed also to anoint Him, whose "head was filled with the drops of night" ( Lu 24:1 ). The myrrh typifies bitter repentance, the fruit of the Spirit's unction ( 2Co 1:21 , 22 ). handles of the lock-- sins which closed the heart against Him.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8258"/><div sID="gen13048" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8258"/><hi type="bold">6. withdrawn--</hi>He knocked when she was sleeping; for to have left her then would have ended in the death sleep; He withdraws now that she is roused, as she needs correction (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.17">Jr 2:17</reference>, 19), and can appreciate and safely bear it now, which she could not then. "The strong He'll strongly try" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.13">1Co 10:13</reference>).<div eID="gen13048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13049" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when he spake--</hi>rather, "because of His speaking"; at the remembrance of His tender words (<reference osisRef="Job.29.2">Job 29:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.29.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Psa 27:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.142.7">142:7</reference>), or till He should speak.<div eID="gen13049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13050" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no answer--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.23.3-Job.9.30">Job 23:3-9; 30</reference>:<reference osisRef="Job.9.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.34.29">34:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.44">La 3:44</reference>). Weak faith receives immediate comfort (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.44">Lu 8:44</reference>, 47, 48); strong faith is tried with delay (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.22">Mt 15:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.23">23</reference>). <div eID="gen13050" type="x-p"/>

"The strong He'll strongly try" ( 1Co 10:13 ). when he spake-- rather, "because of His speaking"; at the remembrance of His tender words ( Job 29:2 , 3 ; Psa 27:13 ; 142:7 ), or till He should speak. no answer-- ( Job 23:3-9; 30 : 20 ; 34:29 ; La 3:44 ). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8259"/><div sID="gen13051" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8259"/><hi type="bold">7. watchmen--</hi>historically, the Jewish priests, &c. (see on <reference osisRef="Song.5.2">So 5:2</reference>); spiritually, ministers (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Is 62:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.17">He 13:17</reference>), faithful in "smiting" (Psalm 141. 5), but (as she leaves them, {v.} 8) too harsh; or, perhaps, unfaithful; disliking her zeal wherewith she sought Jesus Christ, first, with spiritual prayer, "opening" her heart to Him, and then in charitable works "about the city"; miscalling it fanaticism (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.5">Is 66:5</reference>), and taking away her veil (the greatest indignity to an Eastern lady), as though she were positively immodest. She had before sought Him by night in the streets, under strong affection (<reference osisRef="Song.3.2-Song.3.4">So 3:2-4</reference>), and so without rebuff from "the watchmen," found Him immediately; but now after sinful neglect, she encounters pain and delay. God forgives believers, but it is a serious thing to draw on His forgiveness; so the growing reserve of God towards Israel observable in Judges, as His people repeat their demands on His grace. <div eID="gen13051" type="x-p"/>

She had before sought Him by night in the streets, under strong affection ( So 3:2-4 ), and so without rebuff from "the watchmen," found Him immediately; but now after sinful neglect, she encounters pain and delay. God forgives believers, but it is a serious thing to draw on His forgiveness; so the growing reserve of God towards Israel observable in Judges, as His people repeat their demands on His grace.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8266"/><div sID="gen13070" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8266"/><hi type="bold">14. rings set with ... beryl--</hi>Hebrew, Tarshish, so called from the city. The ancient chrysolite, gold in color (Septuagint), our topaz, one of the stones on the high priest's breastplate, also in the foundation of New Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.19">Re 21:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.20">20</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Dan.10.6">Da 10:6</reference>). "Are as," is plainly to be supplied, see in <reference osisRef="Song.5.13">So 5:13</reference> a similiar ellipsis; not as Moody Stuart: "have gold rings." The hands bent in are compared to beautiful rings, in which beryl is set, as the nails are in the fingers. Burrowes explains the rings as cylinders used as signets, such as are found in Nineveh, and which resemble fingers. A ring is the token of sonship (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.22">Lu 15:22</reference>). A slave was not allowed to wear a gold ring. He imparts His sonship and freedom to us (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.7">Ga 4:7</reference>); also of authority (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.42">Ge 41:42</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="John.6.27">Joh 6:27</reference>). He seals us in the name of God with His signet (<reference osisRef="Rev.7.2-Rev.7.4">Re 7:2-4</reference>), compare below, <reference osisRef="Song.8.6">So 8:6</reference>, where she desires to be herself a signet-ring on His arms; so "graven on the palms," &c., that is, on the signet-ring in His hand (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.16">Is 49:16</reference>; contrast <reference osisRef="Hag.2.23">Hag 2:23</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Jer.22.24">Jr 22:24</reference>).<div eID="gen13070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">belly--</hi>Burrowes and Moody Stuart translate, "body." Newton, as it is elsewhere, "bowels"; namely, His compassion (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.14">Psa 22:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.15">Is 63:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.20">Jr 31:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.8">Ho 11:8</reference>).<div eID="gen13071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bright--</hi>literally, "elaborately wrought so as to shine," so His "prepared" body (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.5">He 10:5</reference>); the "ivory palace" of the king (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.8">Psa 45:8</reference>); spotless, pure, so the bride's "neck is as to tower of ivory" (<reference osisRef="Song.7.4">So 7:4</reference>).<div eID="gen13072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sapphires--</hi>spangling in the girdle around Him (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.5">Da 10:5</reference>). "To the pure all things are pure." As in statuary to the artist the partly undraped figure is suggestive only of beauty, free from indelicacy, so to the saint the personal excellencies of Jesus Christ, typified under the ideal of the noblest human form. As, however, the bride and bridegroom are in public, the usual robes on the person, richly ornamented, are presupposed (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.5">Is 11:5</reference>). Sapphires indicate His heavenly nature (so <reference osisRef="John.3.13">Joh 3:13</reference>, "is in heaven"), even in His humiliation, overlaying or cast "over" His ivory human body (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.10">Ex 24:10</reference>). Sky-blue in color, the height and depth of the love of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.18">Ep 3:18</reference>). <div eID="gen13073" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_plain: 16. Literally, "His palate is sweetness, yea, all over loveliness," that is, He is the essence of these qualities. mouth-- so So 1:2 , not the same as "lips" ( So 5:13 ), His breath ( Is 11:4 ; Joh 20:22 ). "All over," all the beauties scattered among creatures are transcendently concentrated in Him ( Col 1:19 ; 2:9). my beloved-- for I love Him. my friend-- for He loves me ( Pr 18:24 ). Holy boasting ( Psa 34:2 ; 1Co 1:31 ).
